utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60/1-A, Momir Nikolic versus the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We would like to make sure that the interpreters are here and that they can hear me. I see the appellant, Mr. Nikolic, is in the courtroom. Mr. Nikolic, can you hear me? THE APPELLANT: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Defence and Prosecution can certainly hear me. Very well. I will now ask for the appearances of the parties. Can we first have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Rock Tansey, and my co-counsel is John Livingston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: My name is Peter Kremer, Mr. President, Marie-Ursula Kind is also with me. I believe that Peter McCloskey, subject to his airplane connections, may also be joining us this morning. And Lourdes Galicia is our case manager; she's also with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. As the registrar announced, the case on our agenda is Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic. This case is before the Appeals Chamber following an appeal launched by the Defence against the sentencing judgement rendered by Trial Chamber I on 2 December, 2003. This morning we will hear the appeal of the Defence, the response of the Prosecution, and if it so wishes, the reply of the Defence. I shall first provide some relevant background to this case. At the plea hearing held on 7 March 2003, Mr. Nikolic pleaded guilty to persecutions, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 3(H) of the Statute of the International Tribunal under Count 5 on the indictment. This count arises out of events that took place in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina as a result of the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica, which was shelled and attacked between 6 and 11 July 1995. Count 5 of the indictment provides that "the crime of persecutions was perpetrated, executed, carried out by and through the following means: (a) the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians, including men, women, and elderly persons; (b) the cruel treatment of Bosnian Muslim civilians, including severe beatings at Potocari and in detention facilities in Bratunac and Zvornik; (c) the terrorising of Bosnian Muslim civilians in Srebrenica and Potocari; (d) the destruction of personal property and the effects belonging to the Muslims; and (e), the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslims from the Serbia enclave." Based on a plea agreement, the Trial Chamber entered a conviction against Mr. Nikolic for Count 5 on the indictment. In the plea agreement, the parties agreed that the Prosecution would recommend to the Trial Chamber a sentence within the range of 15 to 20 years, and the Defence will recommend a sentence of 10 years. The Trial Chamber found that they could not accept the sentences as recommended by either the Defence or the Prosecution. It rather sentenced Mr. Nikolic to 27 years' imprisonment. As stated, this morning we will hear arguments from both parties, but before giving the floor to counsel I will summarise briefly the grounds of appeal launched by the Defence has stated in its written submissions. The first ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred by venturing outside the facts of the guilty plea when assessing the gravity of the offence. The second and 12th ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred when it imposed a sentence of 27 years' imprisonment on Momir Nikolic, since the sentence is inconsistent with the sentences imposed in other cases before the International Tribunal. In his third and fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Nikolic argues that the Trial Chamber double-counted both his role and the vulnerability of the victims as it considered each fact applies that these, in the gravity of the offence, and any is a separate aggravating circumstance. In his fifth ground of appeal, Mr. Nikolic argues that the Trial Chamber erred when it relied upon a mistranslation of the lead Defence counsel's closing argument in weighing the appellant's sentence. In the sixth ground of appeal, the appellant asserts that the Trial Chamber failed to give sufficient credit to the guilty plea, as a mitigating circumstance. Seventh, the appellant claims that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to recognise his full cooperation with the Prosecution. In its eighth ground of appeal, the appellant alleges that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to give him sufficient credit for his expression of remorse. In the ninth, tenth, and eleventh ground of appeal, finally, the appellant submits that he was entitled to greater credit for the mitigating circumstances of his cooperation with the Prosecution prior to his arrest, his good behaviour in the Detention Unit, and his personal circumstances that he was given by the Trial Chamber. I would now like to remind the parties about the standard of review applicable to sentencing appeals. Under Article 25 of the Statute, an appeal is not a trial de novo. The role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting errors of law and invalidating the decision and errors of fact that have occasioned the miscarriage of justice. Trial Chambers are vested with broad discretion to tailor the penalties to fit the individual circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crime. In general, the Appeals Chamber will not revise the sentence unless the Trial Chamber has committed a discernible error in exercising its discretion. Before we proceed, I would also ask the parties to be precise and clear in their submissions and not simply recount what has been set out in their written briefs. In accordance with the Scheduling Order issued by the Appeals Chamber on 19th October, 2005, the appellant shall have up to 30 minutes to make his oral submission. The Prosecution shall then have up to 30 minutes in response to the appellant's submission. And then the appellant shall have up to ten minutes to reply to the Prosecution's response. At the end, Mr. Nikolic has ten minutes to personally address the Appeals Chamber, if he so wishes. So now we will proceed by hearing first from counsel for Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Tansey, please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. It is submitted that the sentence of 27 years was excessive and that there was a discernible error in the Trial Chamber's use of its discretion and/or in the law in sentencing him. We acknowledge at once that the said offence of persecution is a very serious offence, and we wish to make it clear that we do not in any way underestimate its gravity. The appellant relies on all the matters set out at the pleadings, and therefore I shall not repeat them at this stage. As I have said, we submit that the sentence of 27 was excessive and should be reduced, and we note with significance that the Prosecution have consistently maintained, both at trial and subsequent to trial and at this appeal, that the appropriate range of sentence in his case was 15 to 20 years. And by inference, though of course it is not their decision, but by inference the Prosecution are clearly suggesting to the Court that the sentence of 27 years in this case on this appellant was manifestly excessive. And we agree and adopt what the Prosecution have said. On the question of disparity, it is clear from the pleadings that the Prosecution likewise feel that the disparity in sentence imposed on this appellant and other defendants in similarly connected cases merited a review. And so, for example, when dealing with the case of a Mr. Obrenovic, the Prosecution made it clear that there was a substantial similarity between the cases of Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic, and yet there is a massive difference in sentence between the two. Mr. Obrenovic was sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment, and Mr. Nikolic to 27, a difference of ten years. We submit that the Prosecution, in their pleadings at paragraph 42 of the Prosecution response, said this: "The Prosecution acknowledge that there is a disparity between Nikolic's sentence of 27 years and Mr. Obrenovic's of 17 years," in their words, "that is hard to explain." We submit that is a matter of great significance and importance which we would ask Your Honours to take into consideration. The Crown -- the Prosecution say it is hard to explain. We submit, likewise, that on behalf of this appellant we find it on his behalf hard to explain when one compares the two and the other cases. Your Honour, before I deal with particular points, may I just say this: He was, Mr. Nikolic, a teacher, a man with no previous criminal record, a man of good standing in the community, married with two children, and he is now aged 50. He was the Bosnian Serb to publicly admit his guilt in his part in the terrible events which occurred after the fall of Srebrenica. The first of all. There was a public denial in that republic and in Serbia that these horrific events ever took place, that this man had the courage to get up and say: It did take place and I'm guilty of the matters to which, in fact, he has pleaded. He has expressed remorse in meetings before the Chamber and with the Prosecution. And as the Prosecution say, and they have had extensive dealing with him, he has cooperated substantially and extensively with them. And their degree of his cooperation is clearly set out in that. Your Honour, in the Prosecution's supplemental submission before he was sentenced they said: "Mr. Nikolic had cooperated fully with the Prosecution and had provided valuable information regarding the events in and around Srebrenica and even about events in East Bosnia which were beyond the scope of the amended plea agreement on matters relevant to his trial." And in their response for these appeal proceedings, the Prosecution reiterate again - reiterate - the extent of his cooperation. In their words: "He provided substantial cooperation at trial," and they still maintain that he fully cooperated. And that his testimony in their view, with their background knowledge of so much material, of evidences and witnesses and of documentary material, it is their view that his testimony on key issues and events is credible and reliable. And that by virtue of him pleading, he saved the witnesses from testifying about painful and traumatic events. He has contributed to the establishment of the truth and the process of reconciliation. He has shown remorse and he has saved the Tribunal resources by avoiding a lengthy trial. And as far as he is concerned, unlike the other persons involved in the Srebrenica cases, he was a reserve officer. He was a captain. He, in fact, had been a teacher until he was, as a citizen, asked and did and joined the army. He was not a full-time officer, unlike the other persons this -- about whom the Srebrenica cases are concerned. And his rank was considerably lower than those in associated cases of Mr. Krstic, Mr. Obrenovic, and Mr. Blagojevic. He was not a commanding officer. His position in the military was relatively low, and he was not one of the architects, the creators of the criminal joint enterprise. And he never personally passed any order or made any plan nor instigated nor murdered nor participated actively in the murder of any of the victims. And the price that he and his family have had to pay has been enormous. His family have had to leave Bosnia and to be relocated abroad. He, Mr. Nikolic, he is being called by others a traitor to his country, and naturally that weighs very heavily upon him. May I deal then firstly with the -- our submission that the Trial Chamber failed to give sufficient weight or credit to his plea of guilty. We submit that a very substantial reduction in sentence is appropriate to reflect his guilty plea. It was highly significant, as set out in paragraph 142 of the judgement of the Court. It is the first time a Serb has acknowledged criminal responsibility regarding the Srebrenica events." And quoting from a witness from Srebrenica, his admission punched a big hole in the Bosnian wall of denial. And his plea was a significant contribution to the truth and to the advancement of reconciliation. And his account as an insider is of great historic significance. And his plea was entered before trial, not long before trial we acknowledge, so no witnesses nor victims were required to give evidence, and thereby resources saved. And the recognition of the crimes committed provides some form of closure. We submit that his plea of guilty was an act of great courage, and this was confirmed in an open letter by the mayor of Srebrenica, which is set out in paragraph 147. "Momir Nikolic is the first officer of the Serbian army who found the strength and courage to confess the crimes and his participation in them." The Trial Chamber at paragraph 145 says that his plea was significant and accepted can contribute to fulfilling the Tribunal's mandate of restoring peace and promoting reconciliation. They said it was an important factor in mitigation of sentence and was a -- and his guilty plea mitigating because it spared witnesses, as I have said. However, it appears from reading the sentencing judgement that there were two -- or only two real or expressed or implied criticisms regarding the weight to be attached to the plea of guilty. The first implicit criticism is that the plea of guilty only came after the plea agreement had been entered; and secondly, that the saving of resources arising from the plea of guilty cannot be given undue consideration or importance. Dealing with the first criticism, that his plea came only after concluding a plea agreement. We submit that such a criticism is unfair, and we adopt the Prosecution response to the revised appellant's brief at paragraphs 152 and 153, because it is clear that the Prosecution accepted that the timing of his guilty plea should not have worked to his detriment. It states at 152: "The Prosecution notes at the outset that it was not the Prosecution's position that the timing of the guilty plea should work to the detriment of the appellant." In fact, the Prosecution position was at the timing of the plea, though approximately one year after pre-trial disclosure, was important as it came before the start of the trial, and therefore the Prosecution was not required to call several witnesses regarding events in Potocari. And they repeated that at paragraph 153 in their response, and it says, and I quote: "It does not appear that sufficient weight was given to the timing of the plea." We agree with the Prosecution observation and we adopt it. We do not dissent from the proposition that an early guilty plea may have a particular mitigating relevance. However, in considering this specific mattered, the Chamber will be well aware that the indictment in this case was a complicated document, a number of matters as well as counts were included, some of which or one of which he admitted, the others he did not. The documentation in this case was substantial. It had to be carefully considered and analysed before the appellant could enter an informed and considered plea. And in those circumstances, it was reasonable for him to seek, through his lawyers, an agreement to an acceptable guilty plea with the Prosecution. Such matters take time. And we submit that in addition that the Trial Chamber may have failed to appreciate sufficiently the difficulty of the appellant, as a Serb, found in talking about the crimes committed at Srebrenica, given the prevailing denial of responsibility at the time for those events in Serbia and Republika Srpska. Accordingly, considering those factors, we submit that his plea should be considered to be a timely plea for which he should be entitled to full credit. The second criticism was that the saving of Tribunal resources arising from the appellant's plea of guilty carried little weight as a mitigating factor, as paragraph 151 of the sentencing judgement. And at paragraph 67 it said: "The saving of resources cannot be given undue consideration or importance." Well, we agree that the saving of resources should not be given undue consideration, but we submit it should be given proper and due and fair consideration. And it is significant that the Prosecution, likewise, consider, quoting from their response at paragraph 12: "The saving of resources is a relevant and valid factor." And that at paragraph 19 they agree that he's still entitled to credit for the aspect of the timing of the guilty plea relating to the saving of Tribunal resources. And we submit that in practical terms the Trial Chamber's approach on this point was mistaken. Cases before this Tribunal are, in general, it seems, very time-consuming, expensive, and publicly funded. And at a practical level, therefore, being able to dispose of cases by a guilty plea, where appropriate - and I underline where appropriate - is important. And there is a need to encourage defendants to plead guilty where appropriate. And this, we submit, can only be achieved by means of a significant sentencing discount for a plea of guilty. Your Honour, that is our first submission. The second submission -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand the -- The second submission is that the Trial Chamber gave him insufficient credit for his cooperation with the Prosecution, and Rule 101 of the Tribunal specifies that: "Substantial cooperation with the Prosecution before or after conviction is a mitigating circumstance." And it's, as I've already said, the Prosecution has made it clear pre-sentence and post-sentence, that Mr. Nikolic has cooperated fully with the Prosecution. And as they said, as set out at paragraph 153: "He had agreed and testified at the Srebrenica trials, he has agreed to cooperate in relation to the entire wartime period." And their words, which I use: "He has worked hard to answer truthfully and completely all the questions posed to him." And it said this: "Apart from his initial false comments in relation to the Kravica warehouse killings, which he subsequently explained, the Prosecution is unaware of any other false statements made by Mr. Nikolic. And the Prosecution submits that his testimony is credible because it is supported by documentary as well as witness testimony in relation to the VRS offensive in Srebrenica and his role in the coordination of the separation, detention, execution, burial, and re-burial of Muslim prisoners. He was helpful and cooperative. He met the Prosecution. He provided, as I've already said, a lot of information regarding events in and around Srebrenica. He provided information regarding events in Eastern Bosnia. He testified in the Blagojevic and Jokic trial, and he's provided testimony before the Appeals Chamber in Krstic. He has agreed to testify in future proceedings before the Tribunal and provide information in relation to other matters. And the Prosecution position is that Mr. Nikolic fully cooperated and that his testimony on key issues and events is reliable. The Trial Chamber has expressed criticism in its comments, its observations, about Mr. Nikolic. It referred to: (a) numerous instances where the testimony of Mr. Nikolic was evasive," that's the words, "and his willingness to cooperate does not translate into being fully forthcoming in relation to all of the events; (b) in tab B to the amended plea agreement, he admitted he had made false statements, in particular that he ordered executions in Sandici and Kravica, when in fact he had not done so; and (c), criticism, if he was sincere about cooperating, he would have been more open in all aspects of his testimony and had been more forthright in his responses before and to the Trial Chamber; (d) his testimony was not as detailed as it could have been in certain areas, and this is an indicator of the character and a certain lack of candor on the part of Mr. Nikolic. So let us look at these criticisms Nikolic, which we submit are invalid and wrong. Firstly, numerous instances where his evidence was evasive. What is astonishing is that there is only one example cited, and that is in the footnote 252 at page 50. We submit it is wrong in principle to refer to numerous instances without at least putting in the details, either in the main body of the judgement or in the footnotes. And because of this significant omission by the Trial Chamber, it is now not possible to make any assessment as to whether the Trial Chamber was correct in their assessment. And we respectfully remind Your Honours that the obligations under, for example, Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights, that the court should indicate with sufficient clarity the grounds on which they base their decision. And in these circumstances, we submit, there is no evidence to justify the Trial Chamber's assertion that there were numerous instances of evasive evidence by the appellant. And what is again important, to stress, the Prosecution do not suggest that there were numerous instances of evasive evidence by the appellant. As stated in this Trial Chamber's sentencing judgement the Prosecution view was: Apart from his initial false comments in relation to Kravica warehouse, the Prosecution is unaware of any other false evidence. We submit the lack of detail in the judgement of such alleged evasiveness is deeply disturbing. If the Chamber was going to make such observations, especially as the Prosecution view was significantly opposed to the view of the Chamber, it was elementary, fundamental, and essential that the Trial Chamber should have listed in detail the alleged evasiveness. The failure to list details of evasiveness may well be, as we suggest, because there is no evidence of numerous instances where Mr. Nikolic was evasive, and it's -- we submit it appears that the Trial Chamber has misled itself in these observations. The Trial Chamber did refer to the example of, as set out at paragraph 156, and it refers to tab B to the amended plea agreement in which Mr. Nikolic had previously made false statements, namely that he ordered executions at Sandici and Kravica, where he did not. And that was wrong and he acknowledges that, or acknowledged it. But what the judgement fails to state is that it was Mr. Nikolic himself, who shortly having made the statements told the Prosecution -- it was not the Prosecution finding out and in that way he then changed. He went back to them and said that he was sorry, but he in fact had made false statements. And he acknowledged his wrongdoing in making such a statement. He brought it to the attention of the Prosecution and not the other way around. And so in their supplemental submission at paragraph 7 of the 15th of October, 2003, the Prosecutor said: "Other than that one time, Mr. Nikolic has always had a helpful and positive attitude in previous dealings with the Prosecution." And after that, he then, as the Prosecution said: "His cooperation continued to be substantial." He gave evidence in two cases, identified mass graves, stated his willingness to testify in future trials. The third criticism made by the Trial Chamber was this, at paragraph 156 of their judgement: "If he was sincere about cooperating, he would have been more open in all aspects of his evidence, had have been more forthright in his response before and to the Trial Chamber." Rely on the same observations as before. In this case, the Chamber does not even cite one example. It is unclear what the Chamber had in mind, and accordingly it is unclear how these matters could possibly fairly result in any adverse inferences against the appellant. The fourth criticism made by the Chamber: "His testimony was not as detailed as it could have been in certain areas. This is an indicator of his character and certain lack of candor on the part of Mr. Nikolic." As above, the Chamber cited not one example, and accordingly, we submit, it is unclear how these matters could possibly result in adverse inferences against Mr. Nikolic. The Prosecution accept that the Trial Chamber erred, we say, in law by failing to identify the basis of its findings and made no reference to transcripts or other witnesses. And it says: "As there were no examples provided, it is difficult to assess the basis for this reason for diminishing the value of cooperation." And therefore, we submit, that in assessing the agree of cooperation of the appellant, this Appeals Chamber should exclude entirely from its consideration of sentence those matters about which the Trial Chamber provided no evidential material or any important or relevant material. In those circumstances, we submit there is minimal, hardly any evidence of lack of cooperation by Mr. Nikolic, and therefore, he should be entitled to maximum credit for his substantial cooperation. And that he certainly did not receive from the Trial Chamber. The next matter, remorse. We submit the Trial Chamber erred in failing to give him substantial credit for his remorse and his apology to the victims and their families and the Bosniak people, as set out in his statement at paragraph 158(F) of the sentencing judgement. We suggest that statement shows real empathy with the victims and an understanding of the true horror and tragedy of the events of Srebrenica. The Prosecution certainly supported the appellant's submission that he had demonstrated remorse by pleading guilty and had also shown remorse in all their dealings with him. Why did the Trial Chamber, therefore, not give him substantial weight? And there appear to be three reasons, and I shall deal with each in turn. One, and this is set out at paragraph 160 of the sentencing judgement: The Trial Chamber seems to have held against him his explanation of his reasons why he pleaded guilty. Now, we suggest that that is unfair, because the appellant had the honesty to admit that his reasons were an inevitable mixture of self-interest as well as genuine remorse. He expressed his self-interest very clearly, as set out at paragraph 53 of the revised appellant's brief on appeal, page 19. And he said this: "I came to realise that the best solution for me personally would be to enter into an agreement of this kind, to confess my guilt, to testify about the crime. And in that way, quite simply, to save myself, that on the one side; and on the other to help the Court to arrive at the truth, as far as that is possible." That is the clearest expression of self-interest. But in our submission, he was extremely honest about that, which, we submit, is a point in his favour. But he also made it very clear in evidence that he was genuinely remorseful for what had happened. In answer to Judge Argibay at page 1678 to 9 of the evidence as set out in paragraph 58 of the revised appellant's brief he said this: "One of the strongest reasons why I have done all this are my pangs of conscience, a pain I have been carrying inside me all this time. And, believe me, I owe an apology to all the victims, all the children, all the mothers who have lost their sons, and I especially want to apologise to my pupils," he having, as I said, been a teacher. That, we submit, is really genuine remorse. And since the war ended, he had as chief of department of the ministry of refugees and displaced persons issued a large number of decisions for the adaptation and repair of Muslim houses. And as he said, "I did not pay any attention to whether the house was a Serb or a Muslim house to speed up the return of refugees in Bratunac." That's paragraph 59 of the revised appellant's brief. And he made it clear to the Chamber that he was not an extremist and that is confirmed by witnesses who gave evidence before the Tribunal and that in 1992, he said, he had opposed the extremists, and in consequence he had been attacked and hospitalised and had to leave Bratunac. So in 1995, he was naturally concerned something similar might happen to him again. And at the sentencing hearing, long-term friends and colleagues, including a number of non-Serbs, testified that he had friends from different ethnic groups and that he did not discriminate. And a non-Serb student testified that he socialised with Bosniak colleagues and was non-discriminatory towards non-Serb students. We submit there was clear evidence there of genuine remorse for which he should have received greater credit. The second reason at paragraph 160 of the Trial Chamber's judgement -- it said it recalled "his related reason of providing the Prosecution with false information during the plea negotiations." And we submit it's harsh to hold that against him because he was the one who very shortly afterwards went to the Prosecution and told them that he hadn't been honest, and he then apologised. And from that moment onwards, there's no suggestion that he ever told any untruths. And so, we submit that this should not have been held against of him. The third reason given was, as the Court said at note 257, page 51 of the judgement: "The Trial Chamber further recalled that his guilty plea came after one year of full disclosure by the Prosecution's case against him." We submit, and I've given the reasons earlier, that this point should not be held against him. And we adopt the Prosecution observation at paragraph 152 of its response. "The Prosecution notes at the outset that it was not the Prosecution position that the timing of the guilty plea should work to the detriment of the appellant." I accept -- I will not repeat the proposition any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tansey, may I draw your attention to the clock. Your 30 minutes have gone. If you have a couple of minutes more, I can give them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: If I may -- try very swiftly to deal with the question of sentence disparity, and the submission I have made 27 years excessive, when compared with cases reasonably similar backgrounds and when it imposes a sentence outside the range of 15 to 20 years recommended by the Prosecution. May I make it clear, I accept the Court makes the decision and the Prosecution makes the recommendation. But when the Prosecution make such a recommendation, it is one which, in our submission, should command considerable respect. Your Honour, may I just do the comparison of Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Obrenovic was sentenced to the same offence of persecution and pleaded guilty, like this appellant, and cooperated with the Prosecution. He was a career soldier. He was a deputy commander. He was a Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and this brigade was responsible for the municipality in which the vast majority of the executions took place. The acting commander, he was, of the Zvornik Brigade during the two days when many executions took place. And he was responsible, Mr. Obrenovic, for failing to prevent his subordinates from participating in the detention, murder, and burial of Bosnian men. Compare his position and compare Mr. Nikolic. Now, I acknowledge no two cases are exactly the same; there are different facts. But Mr. Nikolic was a reserve officer. He was a captain, not a captain first class, as the Tribunal wrongly described him. He had no command responsibility. His position in the military was relatively low, though I do not suggest unimportant. He had no subordinates. At all times, he was obeying and implementing orders. He personally gave no orders for any person to be killed and he did not kill anyone himself. We submit Mr. Obrenovic was sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment. That was within the range recommended by the Prosecution. Mr. Nikolic got ten years more, though being a much less important figure and with no command responsibility. Your Honour, I see my time is up, and I have to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tansey. Well, if there are no questions from my colleagues, we can move on to the response of the Prosecution -- oh, sorry. I'm sorry, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just one question. Mr. Tansey, assuming that the Trial Chamber made the errors which you allege, can you point to any passage in the sentencing judgement showing that these errors materially affected the appellant's sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, our submission is that what affected the sentence is not, in itself, manifestly clear on the papers themselves. However, where one has errors of such substance in relation to these important matters, for example, the plea of guilty not giving full recognition of that to his substantial cooperation, again not accepting it, and also not acknowledging his remorse, we suggest that the obvious inferences by not accounting for that properly, it inevitably meant to his sentence was going to be higher than it should have been. Your Honour, that is basically how we deal, I hope properly, with Your Honour's observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tansey. I give now the floor to the Prosecution for their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. The submission by Mr. Tansey on behalf of Mr. Nikolic identifies many of the issues that had been canvassed in the briefs, and he articulates very well the concerns that are shared by both parties in respect of the lack of detail provided by the Trial Chamber in justifying the sentence of 27 years and in rejecting the joint submission by the parties for a sentence in the range of 15 to 20 years. The position of the Prosecution is that there has been a discernible error in the exercise of discretion in the imposition of a 27-year sentence on Mr. Momir Nikolic. And in respect of the submissions by Mr. Tansey on Mr. Nikolic's behalf, there is nothing he has said which I take issue with. I plan, in my submissions, just to deal with two errors which I believe are fundamental to the explanation and illustration of how the sentence is in error. And the two points are, one, that the sentences are inconsistent as between perpetrators convicted in connection with the Srebrenica massacre; and secondly, there is disparity of sentence between Momir Nikolic and Obrenovic, who both pled guilty as members of a JCE committing a persecution involving the events of Srebrenica. Both substantially cooperated with the Prosecution and testified against other perpetrators, both at the Blagojevic and Jokic trial and in the Krstic appeal hearing before this Chamber. And there is a disparity of sentence of ten years notwithstanding that there is, in the Prosecution's submission, not justification found in the Trial Chamber to justify the disparity. There were other errors that are commented on in the written materials. One which may have affected the view of the Trial Chamber in assessing sentence is the interpretation error that was alluded to by Mr. Tansey in the beginning. The use of the word "only," in differentiating the Blaskic facts from the Srebrenica facts. I won't deal with it. It's adequately dealt with in the materials but is worth considering, particularly since the Court -- the Trial Chamber was specifically disturbed by the use of the phrase, and I believe all parties are of agreement that that was a translation or interpretation error that was very unfortunate and may have had an influence on the Trial Chamber's assessment of not only the facts, the admissions, but also the sentence. First of all, inconsistent sentence. Why is the sentence of Momir Nikolic inconsistent? And I think it is inconsistent if one examines the history of the Srebrenica sentencing, and it may well be that Momir Nikolic was caught in an unfortunate period of time in the sequence of sentencing. At the time of the sentencing decision, the only Srebrenica sentencing decision was that of Radislav Krstic, a decision on August the 2nd, 2001. General Major Krstic was the commander of the Drina Corps of the Serbian forces. Following orders of General Mladic and the VRS Main Staff, Krstic committed the Drina Corps personnel and resources, mainly from Bratunac and the Zvornik Brigades to the Srebrenica operation, which resulted in the forcible confinement -- I'm sorry, forcible transfer of 25.000 Bosnian Muslims and the execution of over 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men. The evidence at the Trial Chamber and accepted by the Krstic Trial Chamber was that General Krstic supervised the participation of his subordinates in carrying out executions, and after a lengthy trial, General Krstic was convicted of genocide as a participant in the JCE and was sentenced to 46 years' imprisonment. On May 7th, 2003, Momir Nikolic pled guilty to the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity, as a member of a JCE, and that plea was accepted by the Trial Chamber based on the facts set out in the sentencing judgement. Momir Nikolic was a captain in the Bratunac Brigade, responsible for security and intelligence. Momir Nikolic carried out staff functions assigned to him, which included involvement in organising the separation and transfer of the 25.000 Muslim women and children and the segregation of over 7.000 men, knowing of their planned execution by elements of the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades. Srebrenica was a crime of major proportions requiring substantial personnel and resources to carry out. Momir Nikolic's staff role was important and necessary to the carrying out of this crime. But Momir Nikolic was the first Serb to admit to the events of Srebrenica. His guilty plea was combined with substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. He testified at the trial of his superior officer, Colonel Dragan Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and Major Jokic, chief of engineering of the Zvornik Brigade. Nikolic's sentence of 27 years was imposed on December 2nd, 2003. He was the second Srebrenica participant sentenced. And as regard to the benchmark for General Krstic, it may have appeared appropriate. The Prosecution had recommended 15 to 20 years in light of his plea and his cooperation, but events would show, subsequent sentencing decisions would show, that the decision of the Trial Chamber in respect of Momir Nikolic was inconsistent with other sentences. The first evidence of that was the sentencing of Colonel Obrenovic. He pled guilty to persecution, as did Momir Nikolic, as a crime against humanity as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. It was accepted by the same Trial Chamber that sentenced Momir Nikolic on May 21st, 2003, some two and a half weeks later. As acting commander and deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Obrenovic accepted his knowledge of and role in the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians, and this was significant. And if you look at the Obrenovic sentencing decision at, in particular, paragraphs 30 to 34, it is clear that Obrenovic is deeply involved in the events that took place. I'm just going to read from paragraph 33: "Dragan Obrenovic states that he was 'aware that the killing operation was occurring when he was back in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the morning of the 15th of July, 1995.' Dragan Jokic had told him about problems with the burials of prisoners executed and the guarding of prisoners still to be executed." Most of the prisoners that were executed in the Srebrenica operation were executed in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Substantial Zvornik Brigade personnel and resources were needed to carry out the executions and the burials. Obrenovic pled guilty at the same time before the trial as did Momir Nikolic. Obrenovic testified at the trial of his fellow officer, Colonel Dragan Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and his subordinate, Major Jokic, chief of engineering of the Zvornik Brigade. Colonel Obrenovic was sentenced to 17 years on December the 10th, 2003, a mere eight days after the sentencing of Momir Nikolic. There is a disparity in sentence of ten years, yet there is not a word of explanation. In the Obrenovic sentencing to explain why there is a difference of ten years, when by all accounts the responsibility for which both men pled guilty is identical. They both pled guilty to the crime of persecution, to participating as a member of the joint criminal enterprise, and both cooperated fully with the Prosecution and, in the Prosecution's submission, ought to have been sentenced in the same range of sentence. And if Colonel Obrenovic, who was a command officer, received a sentence of 17 years, then it is clear that there is a disparate sentence for Mr. Nikolic when he is sentenced to 27 years. The situation gets a little more complicated as a result of the decision by this Chamber in the Krstic appeal. Major General Krstic appealed from his conviction in sentence for genocide. His conviction for genocide was upheld, not as a participant, but as an aider and abettor, on April 19th, 2004, and his sentence was accordingly reduced to 35 years by the Appeals Chamber. So the adjustment of the Krstic sentence clearly in the comparison of the three sentences where Major General Krstic is in charge of the Drina Corps, in charge of the two brigades that are carrying out the Srebrenica massacre; Colonel Obrenovic is in charge of the Zvornik region. He -- his relative sentence compared to the Krstic sentence has to be taken into account in assessing whether or not the sentence of Momir Nikolic under all of the circumstances is consistent and fair. The crimes of Srebrenica remain the same for all of these perpetrators, whether Krstic, Obrenovic, Blagojevic, Jokic, or Nikolic, the reality is that the JNA forces were involved in the forcible transfer of the 25.000 Muslim civilians and the execution of over 7.000 Muslim men. More recently we had the Trial Chamber decision, the same Trial Chamber that sentenced Momir Nikolic and the same Trial Chamber that sentenced Colonel Obrenovic, in the decision of Blagojevic and Jokic on January 17th, 2005. After a lengthy trial, not a guilty plea, no remorse for Srebrenica, a highly, hotly defended trial, Colonel Blagojevic, who was Momir Nikolic's superior, was convicted of aiding and abetting genocide, persecutions, murder, and other inhumane acts for the forced transfers of the 25.000 Muslim civilians, and a sentence not to more than 27 years but a sentence to 18 years by the same Trial Chamber. So it is clear, I would submit, on the basis of the Blagojevic sentence alone, that no credit was given to Momir Nikolic for his cooperation and no credit was given for his guilty plea. Now, I have to remind this Chamber that the Prosecution has appealed the conviction and sentence of Mr. Blagojevic, but for the time being that is a sentence that can be used as a benchmark for determining the issue before you today. The sentencing decisions subsequent to Momir Nikolic receiving his sentence of 27 years on December 2nd, 2003, raise valid issues of inconsistency and disparity of sentences, given the same crime base and the comparability of roles and relationships of the individual perpetrators. General Major Krstic's sentence was reduced from 46 years to 35 years. He was in a senior command responsibility for the Drina Corps and its units when they committed the Srebrenica genocide. The 27-year sentence of Momir Nikolic is disproportionate, having a regard to Momir Nikolic's staff role and responsibility in the Bratunac Brigade, when combined with his guilty plea and substantial cooperation. Lack of parity in sentencing is best illustrated in the comparison of sentences to Colonel Obrenovic and Colonel Blagojevic, 17 and 18 years respectively. Both are colonels, both are commanders of the two brigades in whose area of responsibility this crime or the Srebrenica crimes took place. Blagojevic commanded the Bratunac Brigade, which was responsible for the logistics of the forcible transfer of the 25.000 Muslim women and children and the guarding and separation of the prisoners for transfer to execution sites, both within Bratunac and the Zvornik Brigade areas of responsibility. Obrenovic and Blagojevic had command responsibility during these events. Momir Nikolic was a captain with staff responsibility. Obrenovic and Momir Nikolic pled guilty and gave substantial cooperation. Blagojevic was convicted after a trial, yet his sentence was nine years lower than Momir Nikolic. It doesn't make any sense, I would submit, that that relationship in sentencing, having regard to the nature of the crime, the command responsibility, and the role of Blagojevic relative to the role of Momir Nikolic. I'm not here to argue the Blagojevic sentence appeal, but in terms of fairness to Momir Nikolic there has to be consistency. A guilty plea and substantial cooperation must be given some credit, given the subsequent sentencing practice by the same Trial Chamber in Obrenovic and Blagojevic and the sentence variance in Krstic by the Appeals Chamber, the sentence of Momir Nikolic is both inconsistent and disparate to all the other Srebrenica sentences and warrants appellant review and reduction. Subject to any questions you may have, those are my submissions. And Mr. McCloskey, I believe, would like to say a few words in respect to the issue of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Yes, I was asking you, before my colleague perfected for me the technology of these instruments, to help me to repair a possible defect in my impression. You referred to there being a joint submission that this sentence should be within the range of 15 to 20 years. Was it the case that your colleagues on the other side proposed a ten-year sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. I misspoke. There was 15- to 20-year recommendation by the Prosecution, and the side office of -- Mr. Nikolic's office asked for ten. I apologise for that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's a privilege to be before the Appeals Chamber. It's not often I get that opportunity. As you know, I was the senior trial attorney involved in the -- in this case and the principal person involved in the plea agreement with Mr. Nikolic. I've been assigned to the Srebrenica case for some nine years now, and as I watched Mr. Nikolic testify, I watched Mr. Obrenovic testify, I'm at a loss to tell you why the sentence disparity. I have tremendous respect for that Trial Chamber. I know those Judges listened very carefully for well over a year and thought very carefully about everything they did, but as what's been pointed out here, you see they're not backing up their issues and their problems with Mr. Nikolic. And again, I'm at a loss to tell you and explain to you why, though, let me offer you one possible explanation. I led both Colonel Obrenovic and Captain Nikolic in evidence. Colonel Obrenovic was a career JNA officer, a very bright man that answered to questions briefly, succinctly, and clearly, without any regard to how it may have made him look or appear. Mr. Nikolic tended to answer questions perhaps more like lawyers would. He -- he was wordier, he went on and on, but I had gotten to know Mr. Nikolic over the year, and that's the way he answered questions. And I listened to him for at least two days and longer under a scathing cross-examination. And he did well. He did well to answer the questions truthfully, and I could point to very few areas where I could identify him not being truthful. That's why we stand here today in support of him. Colonel Obrenovic took responsibility for authorising the death of 3.000 men and boys. He was the commander at the time. He took responsibility for that. Captain Nikolic took responsibility for intending to take part in the joint criminal enterprise, to round those people up and separate them and have them killed. The difference is massive, and I perhaps did not do the job I should have done in convincing the Court in the difference between when a commander takes authority of such a situation and when a staff officer does, but they're very different. Obrenovic did much more than just prevent this execution. If you look at the record and you look at what he pled to, he took responsibility for it. The difference between these two is massive. Now I'll end briefly by emphasising a point that has already been made. Captain Nikolic was the first VRS officer to stand up in front of the world and admit Srebrenica happened and admit his responsibility in it and take responsibility for it. Obrenovic came afterward, and I can tell you Obrenovic was influenced by the fact that Mr. Nikolic got up and did this. And when you look at the record, especially the Muslims, Mr. Nikolic has taken responsibility at this time in history for this institution and for himself, helped the reconciliation of many, many Muslims that I know personally suffered as a result of this. People came up to me constantly, repeatedly, saying that now they could go home, now they have this incredible relief. There's an article of one such Muslim that was written in the New York Times that's part of the record. Read that. You'll get the feeling for how important Mr. Nikolic's plea was to this institution, to this case, to Bosnia, and to reconciliation. And I say that in all candour and honesty, and I'll look into each one of your eyes, there is no question that what he did was very important for this case and the people of Bosnia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. This does conclude the response of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Kremer. Now may I turn to the Defence for their reply. You have ten minutes, Mr. Tansey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. May I say, I'm very grateful to my learned friends for what they have said, and I have nothing to add to those observations. One matter which I'd hoped to address you upon before was not merely the question of disparity, but the question of the gravity of the offence and aggravating features. May I say, this doesn't arise in reply to what my learned friends have said because they haven't specifically dealt with it. It was the question -- and if I may with Your Honours' leave actually just deal with this point, because we're concerned or have been concerned that there is a question of a certain form of double-counting, that what in fact has happened is that, Your Honour, if I say at paragraph 139 of the sentencing judgement it says: "The Trial Chamber finds that the following aggravating circumstances have been proven beyond reasonable doubt: The position of authority and role of Momir Nikolic and the vulnerability of the victims." And our submission is this: That they should not have been considered to have been aggravating factors because they had already been considered to be part of the gravity of the offence. And if I may just deal very briefly with this point. At paragraph 103 of the sentencing judgement the Trial Chamber says as follows: "In assessing the gravity of the offence, the Trial Chamber considers it appropriate to first examine the crime of persecutions in this case, the underlying criminal conduct, and the specific role played by Momir Nikolic in its commission." So clearly, role is being considered as part of the gravity of the offence. "And also take into account the status of the victims of the criminal activity." Now, we submit that if one looks carefully at particular aspects or particular paragraphs of the judgement, that the factors that the Tribunal has deemed to be aggravating have, in our submission, been incorporated, in fact, in the gravity of the offence. Your Honour, if I might cite particular examples for Your Honours' assistance. I referred to paragraph 103. Paragraph 104 the Tribunal says: "When assessing the gravity of the offence, the Trial Chamber must also consider the role that he played in the commission of the crime." And further down at paragraph 114: "The Chamber will examine Mr. Nikolic's formal functions and actual duties." And this is all part of the assessment of the gravity of the offence. In addition, in its findings at paragraph 121 the Trial Chamber says: "In making its determination regarding the gravity and nature of the offence has reviewed the evidence before it and has considered the purpose in which Mr. Nikolic was a participant and his role." And it sets out the very aspects at paragraph 123 how he -- his coordinating role, separate, transportation, et cetera. And, Your Honour, in our submission -- having considered these particular matters it then says at paragraph 124, and these are all matters part of its analysis of the gravity of the offence it says this. It says: "It finds a sentence in the range of 20 years to life to be appropriate based solely on the gravity of the crime committed by Momir Nikolic, his role and participation in the commission of that crime." And we submit, therefore, that when one actually looks at the particular paragraphs in question to which I have referred, that in fact the factors which the Tribunal deem to be aggravating factors, in fact, were included in its own analysis of what constitutes the gravity of the offence. And therefore, our concern is that in the case there may well have been double-counting in the case, and if that is the case, then clearly it would have wrongly added to the sentence imposed upon him. Your Honour, may I just deal with the final matter then, and it relates, in fact, to the matter at paragraph 122. It is a matter that has concerned the appellant personally very much as well. In its judgement at paragraph 122, the trial -- it reads: "The Trial Chamber has examined the crime of persecutions for which Momir Nikolic has admitted responsibility. The Trial Chamber was shocked to hear the Nikolic Defence state that only 7.000 men, only Muslim men, as opposed to all non-Serbs, from only one municipality were murdered. The comparison is not helpful to assess the gravity of the offence and the use of the term 'only' in relation to the number of persons murdered is shameful." Had counsel said that, it would have been shameful, but he didn't say that. It's an unfortunate mistranslation that what he said was, effectively, "around 7.000 people." Now, the consequence was and the rebuttal was this was never taken up with counsel at the time, as one would have expected, are you saying only, do you mean that? We submit that in fact the fact that the Tribunal made this reference and repeated shocked and shameful may well -- the Tribunal may well have thought that these thoughts emanated, came from Mr. Nikolic, part of the team, which in fact was the last thing that they ever had said. And it may be, and we understand that Judges are deemed to exclude such matters from their mind, that it may be that this misinterpretation created a sense of hostility and anger towards the Nikolic Defence, and it may well have affected their judgement as well in determining the sentence imposed upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless there's any other matter in which I can assist you upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I thank you, Mr. Tansey, for your reply. So this concludes the consideration of the submission of the parties. Now, may I turn to Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Nikolic, if you so wish, you have up to ten minutes to -- for a personal statement to address personally the Court. You have the floor, Mr. Nikolic. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would, with this address, like to express my sincere remorse and regret about the awful crimes that took place after the fall of Srebrenica. I would like to express particular respect towards the victims because of the terrible crimes against their families, their brothers, sisters, friends, who have to now live without these people and whose suffering will never end. I would like to convince this Honourable Court that I did not have any enemies among the Muslims. Quite the contrary. I had many friends with whom I spent my whole life. Amongst -- many of my students were Muslims. I was their professor in high school, and they respected me and loved me, just as I respected and loved them. I am particularly sad and feel special pain because I am aware that some of my students were killed in this crime, and I was not able to help them. It is even more awful to know, and it is even more painful to know, that you, in some way, contributed with your own acts to this crime. I would like, Your Honours, to tell you that I never militarily participated in this war. I myself was expelled in 1992, and I was a refugee in Serbia. I was expelled because I disagreed with the SDS authorities. I was physically abused, and I ended up in the hospital. After therapy, which lasted for six months, I was forcefully mobilised by the authorities in Serbia, and I was force -- transferred by force to -- back to Srebrenica. Aware of the gravity of the crime that occurred after the fall of Srebrenica, I decided to admit my guilt, to accept my guilt, and to be adequately punished. I would like to inform this Honourable Court that I am a captain in the reserve, that I never attended any meetings or actively participated in any meetings at which decisions were taken about the fate of the people in Srebrenica. I also never actively participated in any other meetings held after the fall of Srebrenica when decisions were made about the fate of the people of Srebrenica. My role in any of the meetings was to create conditions for the participants to be able to discuss matters quietly and in peace. My professional tasks were what I was doing in this respect, and they do not constitute any crimes. Everything that I did was done on the basic of -- on the basis of superior orders, and I did -- I never did anything of my own accord. Your Honours, I am not accused of command responsibility, but for individual acts. As part of my individual responsibility or guilt, I never personally abused anybody, physically or verbally, I never killed anyone. I did not attend or see any particular killing. I never ordered anyone to abuse or kill anyone, and I never incited anyone to commit any crime. Besides the facts that I have just stated, it is also true that I am a captain in the reserve in a light infantry brigade, and it is not authorised to process the perpetrators of criminal act. Based on the above, it can be concluded that I did not have any authority or power and could not have been in the centre of events because I never in any way decided about anything, I did not have subordinate units which would be in a position to carry out any such orders. In all of the situations in question, I conveyed the orders of superiors, and I assisted in the implementation of orders. In my case, the decisions referred to the forcible transfer from Potocari to the free Muslim territory. Your Honours, I do not wish in any way to minimise my responsibility, but I would like you to properly assess my role and my responsibility as a reserve officer who was not in command, who did not plan, did not organise or order anything, did not kill or abuse anyone, and was not an authorised person who could prosecute the perpetrators of criminal acts. And finally, Your Honours, I would like to inform you that I am prepared, in coming trials which relate to Srebrenica, to testify at the invitation of the Court about the events, according to my best recollection. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. You may sit down. This concludes today's hearing. I would like to express my appreciation to the parties for their submissions and a very good conduct of the proceedings, and a particular thanks to the interpreters for their excellent work. The hearing stands adjourned.
